title: Nullable value types vs nullable references (struct wrapper vs annotation)
hook: The same `?` suffix means two different things in C#. On numbers and dates it is a real struct that can be empty; on strings and classes it is a note for the compiler only.

blocks.text: C# uses one punctuation mark — `?` — for two separate null stories. On a **value type** like `int` or `DateTime`, `T?` is shorthand for `System.Nullable<T>`, a struct that stores either a value or an empty state. On a **reference type** like `string` or a custom class, `T?` is a **nullable reference type (NRT)** annotation: it tells the compiler the variable might hold a null reference, but it does not create a new Common Language Runtime (CLR) type.

entries.plainDefinition: A struct wrapper that lets a value type (int, bool, DateTime) represent “no value” without using a reference.
entries.example: `int? score = null;` means HasValue is false.

entries.plainDefinition: A compiler-only marker on reference types. `string?` and `string` are the same CLR type; the `?` changes warnings, not memory layout.
entries.example: `string? json = redis.Get(key);` warns if you use `.Length` without a check.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET runtime that executes your compiled code. It has always allowed null references on classes; NRT does not change that.
entries.example: A null `string?` still throws NullReferenceException at run time if you dereference it.

entries.plainDefinition: On `Nullable<T>`, returns true when a real value is stored and false when the nullable is empty.

blocks.text: Mixing these two meanings causes real bugs. A CSV import with an empty score column should use `int?`, not `0` (which looks like a real score). A Redis cache miss should be `string?`, not an empty string sentinel that collides with valid data. In interviews, saying “`string?` is a different type at run time” is wrong — only `int?` is a different CLR type.

blocks.title: Quick discriminator
blocks.body: If `T` is a struct (`int`, `DateTime`, `bool`), `T?` is `Nullable<T>` — real runtime type. If `T` is a class or interface, `T?` is an annotation — same runtime type as `T`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: From source code to run time

items.title: Write `int?` or `string?` in source
items.body: Both use the `?` suffix, but the compiler resolves them differently based on whether the underlying type is a value type or reference type.

items.title: Compiler emits IL (Intermediate Language)
items.body: `int?` becomes `System.Nullable<int>` in the assembly. `string?` becomes `System.String` — identical to plain `string`.

items.title: Just-In-Time compiler (JIT) runs the code
items.body: Nullable structs live on the stack or inline in objects. Null references are still null pointers on the heap — NRT never adds a wrapper.

items.title: Use checks at boundaries
items.body: Test `HasValue` or use `??` for value types. Use `is not null` or `?.` for reference types before dereferencing.

diagram.title: Two paths for the same ? suffix
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  Q[You write T?] --> VT{T is a value type?}
  VT -->|yes| ST[Nullable struct at run time]
  ST --> HV[HasValue / Value / ??]
  VT -->|no| AN[Annotation only at compile time]
  AN --> WARN[Compiler warns on unsafe use]
  AN --> NRE[NullReferenceException still possible at run time]

snippet.label: Optional CSV score as int?
snippet.explanation: Line 3: empty cells return null — HasValue is false. Line 7: `??` converts the nullable struct to a plain `int` for the rest of the pipeline.

snippet.label: Lifted operators on int?
snippet.explanation: Line 4: arithmetic operators are “lifted” — if any operand is null, the result is null. Lines 5–6: `<` with null is false (a common interview trap); `== null` is the reliable test.

snippet.label: string? is still System.String at run time
snippet.explanation: Line 2: non-nullable parameters — assigning null is a warning. Line 5: return type `string?` models a missing value. Line 8: pattern match narrows null-state so `.Length` is safe.

blocks.title: Nullable models in C# vs JS/TS
rows: `int?` is a real struct with HasValue
No built-in struct; use `number | null` or `undefined`
`string?` is annotation only; run time is still null
`string | null` is erased; run time is still null
Boxes to a null object reference, not a boxed struct

blocks.title: Using 0 or empty string as “missing”
blocks.body: An empty CSV cell is not the same as a score of zero. A Redis miss is not the same as an empty string token. Use `int?` and `string?` to model absence, then coalesce at the boundary.

blocks.title: Assuming T? in generics is always a reference annotation
blocks.body: On an unconstrained generic `T`, `T?` means “default if T is a struct, nullable annotation if T is a class.” That is why APIs use `MaybeNull` attributes instead of returning `T?` blindly.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: int? is Nullable<int> — HasValue and Value at run time; null string? is a missing reference with the same System.String type. Lifted nullable arithmetic returns null when any operand is null — SQL-style three-valued logic in CSV grade math. Boxing null Nullable<T> yields null object reference, not a boxed zero. Redis cache miss: model as string? not empty string unless empty is a valid stored value. TypeScript undefined has no C# twin on references — only null plus HasValue on structs.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying string? is a different CLR type from string. Using 0 or "" as missing when int? or string? is correct. Calling .Value on null int? without HasValue. Equating JS undefined with int?.

interviewTakeaways: int? is Nullable<int> at run time; string? is String with an annotation.
Lifted operators on nullable value types propagate null.
Boxing null Nullable<T> produces null object, not boxed default.
60s: Value types use Nullable<T>. References use annotations. Do not use 0 for missing. HasValue before .Value.
Follow-up: how does ?? differ for int? versus string?
commonPitfalls: string? as different CLR type — rejected in senior interviews.
0 or empty string instead of int?/string? for missing data.
Strong answer: 'Nullable<T> struct vs reference annotation. HasValue gate. Model Redis miss as null not empty unless valid.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript unions are erased at run time. C# `int?` is a real struct; `string?` is erased like `string | null` in TypeScript.
JavaScript has two “empty” values. C# has one `null` plus `HasValue` on nullable structs. Missing CSV cells map cleanly to `int?`.
